lesson.title: From Alarm to Automatic Lock
lesson.summary: An intrusion prevention system, or IPS, uses detection techniques much like an IDS but sits inline with traffic and actively blocks what it identifies as malicious, rather than only alerting.
lesson.body:
An intrusion prevention system builds directly on everything an intrusion detection system does: the same signature based and anomaly based techniques for recognizing malicious traffic. The difference is what happens the moment something suspicious is identified. Where an IDS logs the event and alerts a human, an IPS is positioned inline, directly in the path of the traffic, so it can drop the malicious packet, reset the connection, or block the offending source outright, all automatically, before that traffic ever reaches its intended destination.

This inline positioning is the key architectural difference, and it comes with a real tradeoff. Because an IDS typically watches a copy of traffic off to the side, a false positive, legitimate traffic incorrectly flagged as malicious, costs nothing but a noisy alert that a person can review and dismiss. Because an IPS sits directly inline and acts automatically, a false positive there can actually block legitimate traffic and disrupt real users or services. This is exactly why organizations don't automatically prefer an IPS over an IDS in every situation: the speed and automation of active blocking is extremely valuable against fast moving attacks, but it raises the stakes of getting the detection logic wrong, since a mistake can now cause an outage rather than just an ignored alert.

In practice, the two are often layered together rather than treated as a strict either or choice. Some traffic may pass through an IPS configured aggressively for well understood, high confidence attack patterns, where blocking automatically is low risk, while other, less certain signals are still routed to an IDS style alerting workflow so a person makes the final call. Understanding both matters because they represent two different philosophies for the same underlying detection engine: alert and let a human decide, or detect and act immediately, and the right choice depends on how confident the detection is and how costly a wrong automatic decision would be.
